Reading the recording twice as fast halves its duration and raises its pitch in ordinary resampling.
That describes slower playback.
Ordinary speed changes do not preserve both.

tryIt: Calculate how a two-second recording would change at half and double speed. Then compare with an original recording you control.

glossary.fit: Adjusts a sample to match its event duration.
glossary.loopAt: Adjusts sample speed to fit a chosen number of cycles.
glossary.resampling: Playing a recording at a changed reading speed, linking duration and pitch changes.
glossary.playback speed: How fast a recording is read relative to its original rate.

title: Make an arrangement you can reproduce
goal: Turn a generative sketch into a deliberate, reviewable study.
explain: An advanced pattern is not advanced merely because it has many functions. It is advanced when you can explain its structure, control its variation, diagnose it, and choose what to keep. For a reproducible study, write explicit pitches and schedules for the moments that must repeat exactly.

Plan three versions of one motif: plain, transformed, and reduced. Give each a place in a form and make a listening checklist before running it. Check the cycle count, the main arrival, the bass register, and whether added layers obscure the motif. Save code and environment notes together so a later version can be investigated rather than guessed at.

example.title: Read it, then predict it
example.text: This twelve-cycle form returns to the motif after a two-cycle reduction. Its one scheduled reversal is intentional and inspectable; no chance decision determines the main section boundary.

practice.question: Which evidence best supports calling your arrangement controlled?
options: You can explain and predict its important events, then verify them by listening
It uses the loudest possible settings
feedback: Prediction, observation, and revision show practical control.
Completeness of function usage is not a composition goal.
Loudness is not structural understanding.
Revision is a normal part of skilled work.

tryIt: Create a 12- or 16-cycle original study with a clear motif, one derived variation, and a deliberate gap. Document tempo convention, source sounds, and required packages. After listening, make one evidence-based revision and explain the trade-off.

glossary.reproducibility: Being able to recreate and explain the intended result with saved code and setup notes.
glossary.motif: A short recognizable musical idea that can be repeated and developed.
glossary.arrangement: The placement and changing roles of musical parts over time.
glossary.revision: A deliberate change made after evaluating a draft.

title: Code order is not a pedalboard
goal: Separate pattern operations from fixed audio-engine routing.
explain: Pattern operations can depend strongly on their order. But writing audio controls in a different dot order does not freely rewire Strudel’s Web Audio effects. The engine has a documented processing order, and repeated settings for a single-use effect can overwrite earlier settings.

For example, two lpf calls do not create two low-pass filter stages around another effect. The later cutoff setting replaces the earlier value for that control. When a result surprises you, inspect whether you are changing pattern structure, assigning control values, or requesting an audio effect. Those are three different kinds of operation.

example.title: Look closely at one idea
example.text: The final low-pass cutoff here is 1800 Hz. This is not “filter at 400, distort, then filter again at 1800.” Read the official signal-chain reference before assuming custom routing.

practice.question: Why is this not a two-filter serial chain?
options: The later lpf assigns the same single-use control again
feedback: D3 specifies a pitch.
Dots still chain operations and settings.
The issue is duplicate control assignment, not an automatic mute.
The engine’s fixed routing and control assignment differ from building arbitrary pedal stages.

tryIt: Compare the example with one that keeps only lpf(1800). Explain why you should check the engine’s signal-chain rules before designing an effect-order experiment.

glossary.signal chain: The order in which generated audio passes through processing stages.
glossary.lpf: The low-pass cutoff control, not a request to add unlimited separate filter instances.
glossary.distort: A distortion effect that adds nonlinear tone coloration.
glossary.overwrite: Replace an earlier assigned control value with a later value.
